title: To whom shall we go (John 6:60–69)
hook: many walk away; Peter says thou hast the words of eternal life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hardest words in John six: my flesh is meat indeed. Your line was eat, and live. What did you notice actually feeds you? Day five hundred five, and a new week.

It ends in a synagogue in Capernaum. John says that's where Jesus taught all of it: the bread, the flesh, the blood. And it costs him. Not the crowd from the hillside this time. His own disciples, people who had been following him, start to leave. Some of them may have eaten the loaves by the lake. Now they're going home. Jesus watches them go. He doesn't call them back. He doesn't run after them with a softer version. Then he turns to the twelve who are still standing there and asks them a question that leaves the door wide open.
screen: `A SYNAGOGUE IN CAPERNAUM.` → `HIS OWN DISCIPLES WALK OUT.` → `HE TURNS TO THE TWELVE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a complaint, in the Douay-Rheims: "This saying is hard, and who can hear it?" Not just hard to understand. Hard to accept. Jesus knows they're murmuring, and he doesn't take it back. He says the words he has spoken are spirit and life, and that some of them don't believe. And then: "After this many of his disciples went back; and walked no more with him." Went back, walked no more with him. Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will you also go away?" Not a threat. A real question. He lets them choose. And Peter answers, the way Peter usually does, first and from the gut: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Notice what Peter doesn't say. He doesn't say, I understand it all now. He doesn't say, it isn't hard. He doesn't even say, I'm sure. He says: where else would we go? It's the faith of someone who has looked at the alternatives and can't walk away from these words. Then he adds: we have believed and have known that thou art the Christ, the Son of God. Some Catholics turn to this line on days when the teaching is hard, or the Church is hard to love, or God is silent. Staying isn't the same as having no questions. Peter will deny Jesus three times before the story ends. But here, when it costs something, he stays.
screen: `THIS SAYING IS HARD.` · `MANY WALKED NO MORE WITH HIM.` · `WILL YOU ALSO GO AWAY?` · `WHERE ELSE WOULD WE GO?` · then, large: `THOU HAST THE WORDS OF ETERNAL LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay when it's hard. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're tempted to walk away from. A commitment, a friendship, a practice, a hard conversation, maybe even this path. Don't decide anything right now. Just stay with it for the length of the bell. Notice the urge to get up and go, and don't follow it, just this once. If you pray, you can use Peter's words: Lord, to whom shall we go? If you don't, just stay, and notice what staying feels like. The bell holds the time.
To whom shall we go. Peter's answer when many disciples walked away and Jesus asked the twelve if they'd go too. Today's word.

what it means: Peter stays not because it's easy but because there's nowhere else to find these words.
what a scholar hears: 'many walked no more with him' is John 6:66 in most Bibles, 6:67 in the Douay; some readers hear Peter's confession here as John's counterpart to Caesarea Philippi.

notes: Week seventy-three begins (days 505–511); the review notes the new week.
Verse numbering: the Douay runs one higher than the KJV/NABRE in John 6 after 6:51; refs give both. Confirm.

Peter's confession: the Douay (following the Vulgate) reads 'thou art the Christ, the Son of God' in 6:70; many modern critical texts read 'the Holy One of God'. The voice paraphrases the Douay. Consider a note in a later edition.
